problem.title: Pump failure prediction
problem.context: A water utility runs about 400 pumps in 12 pumping stations. Each pump has vibration, temperature and pressure sensors that report every second. When a pump fails without warning, part of the town loses its water supply, so the utility wants to replace bearings and seals before they fail. Several stations are in rural areas with an unreliable mobile connection. The utility has two data scientists and relies on its IT department for servers and networks.

requirements.text: Warn the maintenance team at least 24 hours before a pump is likely to fail, naming the pump and the probable cause.
Improve the predictions as technicians record what they find at each inspection.
When a station loses its connection for up to two days, warnings for its pumps still reach the station's on-call technician.
When a new pump model is installed, its pumps get predictions within one month, without changes to how the other pumps are scored.
Sensor data stays on the utility's own premises: no cloud service may store or process it.

points.description: The utility stores and processes data on premises, trains a shared fleet model centrally, and deploys pump-family adapters for station-edge inference. Stations issue local warnings during outages and buffer results for up to 48 hours, after which synchronized data and inspection labels support batch retraining. Trade-off: This preserves utility data control and warning availability while reusing a common model across pump families. It gives up rapid feedback and potentially fresh model updates, because labels arrive through inspections and synchronization may be delayed; maintaining adapters also adds coordination overhead.

points.description: Station equipment runs autonomous inference and learning on premises, using a model tailored to each pump family. It issues local warnings during outages, retains incremental updates locally, and synchronizes them later within the utility’s owned processing and storage environment. Trade-off: This improves local responsiveness, outage resilience, and data control, but requires maintaining multiple pump-family models and managing delayed synchronization. Learning and operational visibility may be less consistent across stations until updates are exchanged.

adrs.title: Where should scoring and outage handling run?
adrs.context: The utility requires warnings to reach station staff during up to two days without a connection, and sensor data must remain within utility premises. Central-only scoring keeps processing centralized but cannot deliver a warning over a failed link. Both hybrid and autonomous station scoring meet the data boundary while allowing local alerts.

adrs.title: How should models use inspection findings and accommodate new pump families?
adrs.context: Predictions need useful lead time and probable causes, technician findings must improve them, and a new pump model must receive predictions within one month without changing existing scoring. Shared models can reuse fleet learning, while family-specific extensions can isolate new equipment. Local learning is responsive but needs validation; batch learning is controlled but may delay updates. Predictive accuracy and onboarding time require operational evidence.
